title: Big numbers and prices
intro: The numbers you need for real prices, and the words for cheap, expensive and more. Plus: why you will almost never see a Vietnamese coin.

words.hook: A hundred chums squeezed onto one bench, all humming one calm, level "chum".
words.tip: In Hà Nội, tr sounds like ch, so trăm sounds like "chum". ă is a short, quick a. Keep the tone level.
words.fact: Trăm năm, a hundred years, means a lifetime. The great poem Truyện Kiều opens with it: "Trăm năm trong cõi người ta".
words.note: trăm is 100: hai trăm nghìn is 200.000₫. Not triệu, a million.
words.remember: trăm is a hundred; in prices it nearly always means hundreds of thousands: hai trăm is 200.000₫, a good dinner for two, not a bánh mì.

words.hook: Say "sing in" and drop the "si": "ngin". A thousand singers, every voice sinking low.
words.tip: ngh is the ng of "sing" (written ngh before i, e and ê). The huyền tone falls gently. The South says ngàn.
words.fact: Hà Nội says nghìn; the South says ngàn. Both mean a thousand.
words.note: nghìn is 1.000, the last word of most prices: năm mươi nghìn is 50.000₫.

words.hook: A million mosquitoes squeal "chee-ew" in one quick beat, and each bite lands with a heavy thud, like the nặng tone.
words.tip: In Hà Nội, tr sounds like ch. iê glides from "ee" to "eh", then u. Nặng drops low and stops short in the throat.
words.fact: A millionaire is a triệu phú: triệu, million, plus phú, rich.
words.note: triệu is a million: một triệu is 1.000.000₫, and the biggest note is 500.000₫. Not trăm (100) or nghìn (1.000).

words.hook: A 20.000₫ note says hai mươi nghìn: mươi is the -ty, calm and level. Ten on its own, mười, sighs down.
words.tip: Like mười, but level: no fall.
words.note: After mươi, 1 becomes mốt: hai mươi mốt is 21. At stalls people drop nghìn: "Năm mươi!" means 50.000₫, and menus write 50k.
words.fact: In quick Hà Nội speech mươi often disappears: hai mốt for 21, ba lăm for 35.

words.en: five, after the tens (as in 15 and 25)
words.hook: A lamb takes the five's place in 15, 25 and 35; say it short, like "lum" (rhymes with "chum"), calm and level. Leave năm there and hai mươi năm means "twenty years".
words.tip: ă is short. Keep it level.
words.fact: Many Hà Nội speakers say nhăm instead of lăm after the tens: hai mươi nhăm, 25.
words.note: lăm takes the place of năm after mười or mươi: mười lăm is 15, hai mươi lăm 25. Sellers often shorten it: hai lăm.
words.remember: lăm is a five that follows a ten: mười lăm 15, hai mươi lăm 25, often said hai lăm. A five on its own or at the start is năm: năm nghìn, 5.000.

words.en: zero (for an empty tens place, as in 105)
words.hook: Picture 1_5 with an empty slot in the middle, where a tiny bell rings one flat "ling".
words.tip: Hà Nội says một trăm linh năm for 105; the South says lẻ. In Hà Nội, linh sounds close to English "ling". Keep the tone level.
words.fact: Years are read as whole numbers, not in pairs: 2005 is hai nghìn không trăm linh năm, casually hai nghìn linh năm.

words.note: It follows the unit: hai nghìn rưỡi is 2,500; một tiếng rưỡi is an hour and a half.
words.hook: Your voice cracks halfway through the word, just as the number breaks into a half.
words.tip: In Hà Nội, r sounds like z. ươi glides from ư to ơ to i. The ngã tone breaks in the middle, then jumps up.
words.fact: Time works the same way: hai giờ rưỡi is half past two.
words.remember: rưỡi always comes after a unit and adds half of it: trăm rưỡi 150, nghìn rưỡi 1.500, một cân rưỡi a kilo and a half. Hear rưỡi, look at the word before it.

words.hook: Slide "tee" into "ten" in one syllable: tiền, a sad falling sigh as your money leaves your wallet.
words.tip: t has no puff of air. iê glides from "ee" to "eh". The huyền tone falls gently.
words.fact: At Tết, children and grandparents get tiền mừng tuổi: crisp new notes in red envelopes, for luck. The South says lì xì, from Cantonese.

words.hook: Ding-DONG: the doorbell's second note sinks, like huyền. It is the landlord, and he wants your đồng.
words.tip: đ is a firm d with the tongue behind the top teeth. ô is tighter than the o of English "dong", and in Hà Nội the lips close at the end, so it sounds close to "dohm".
words.fact: đồng still means copper or bronze in everyday words: a bronze drum is a trống đồng, like the famous drums of the ancient Đông Sơn culture.

words.hook: "Bow, new." You bow to the seller and, keeping your voice flat, ask how much the new thing costs.
words.tip: nh is like the ny in "canyon". Both syllables stay level.
words.fact: At markets many prices are not written down. "Bao nhiêu tiền?" opens a friendly negotiation.

words.hook: "Dut!" (rhymes with "but") you yelp as the price shoots up, just like the rising tone.
words.tip: ă is short. The final t is cut off, not released. The South says mắc.
words.fact: "Đắt quá!" with a smile is the classic opening move when haggling.
words.note: Đắt quá! Too expensive! The opposite is rẻ, cheap. Northern đắt; the South says mắc.
words.remember: đắt is the complaint: Đắt quá! Too expensive! Its opposite is rẻ, cheap, and what you ask for next is bớt, take some off.

words.hook: It is so cheap your voice drops low in disbelief, "zeh...": really, that cheap?
words.tip: In Hà Nội, r sounds like z. e is open, like the e in "bed". Hỏi starts at your normal pitch and drops further and faster than huyền; said alone it may lift a little at the end. The hỏi mark is a question mark without its dot.
words.fact: Two market proverbs: "Của rẻ là của ôi" (cheap goods are stale goods) and "Tiền nào của nấy" (you get what you pay for).

words.en: -er; more (after the describing word: cheap + more = cheaper)
words.hook: Say British "her" with an n on the end: hơn, a little more. Round your lips and it becomes hôn, a kiss, which is more than a hug.
words.tip: ơ is the vowel of British "fur" with no r; ô is a tight, rounded o. Keep the tone level.
words.note: It goes after the describing word: rẻ hơn is cheaper, đắt hơn is more expensive.
words.fact: hơn also works for people: cao hơn is taller, đẹp hơn is more beautiful.

words.hook: Oliver Twist holds up his bowl for more; his voice cracks, then jumps: "Nữa!"
words.tip: ưa glides from ư ("oo" with spread lips) to a short "uh". The ngã tone breaks, then jumps high.
words.fact: "Một bát nữa!" (one more bowl!) is a fine thing to say at a phở stall; bát is the Northern word for bowl.
words.note: nữa is more: một cốc nữa, one more glass. Not nửa, half.

grammar.title: Big numbers, biggest part first
grammar.text: Numbers go biggest part first, with mươi for the tens from 20 up (10 to 19 use mười): hai trăm năm mươi is 250. After mười or mươi, 5 becomes lăm: hai mươi lăm is 25. An empty tens place is linh: một trăm linh năm is 105.

combos.vi: Phở gà bốn mươi lăm nghìn
combos.note: Spoken fast: bốn lăm nghìn, and many Hà Nội speakers say bốn nhăm.

combos.vi: Bún cá ba mươi lăm nghìn

combos.note: Not 25: after mươi, five is lăm. With năm it means years.
Literally "how much money?". The standard way to ask a price.
quá after a word means "so", as in Ngon quá!

feature.title: Copper, paper, plastic
feature.dek: The đồng is named after a metal you will never see in your change. A short history of Vietnamese money, and the market that has sold Hà Nội everything since 1889.
feature.pull: Vietnam brought coins back in 2003. By 2011 it had given up.
feature.intro: The đồng is named after copper, a metal you will almost never find in your change. This issue follows Vietnamese money from coins to plastic, along with the numbers you need to spend it.

beats.text: Emperor Lý Thái Tổ made this place his capital in 1010 and named it Thăng Long, "ascending dragon". In 2010 the city celebrated a thousand years, một nghìn năm, since that day. It has only been called Hà Nội since 1831.
With so many zeros, Hà Nội shortens prices. A bowl of phở is "năm mươi", fifty, with the nghìn (thousand) left unsaid, and menus write 50k.
Rent, wages and motorbikes are counted in triệu, millions. The largest note, 500,000 đồng, is blue, like the 20,000: count the zeros before you pay.

Đồng is the Sino-Vietnamese word for copper, the metal of the old coins. Coins came back in 2003, but people never took to them, and in 2011 the State Bank stopped issuing them. Between 2003 and 2006 every note from 10,000 đồng up moved to polymer, a plastic that survives the monsoon.

For the full experience, try Đồng Xuân market in the Old Quarter (a different đồng, not copper). The French set it up in 1889, thirteen years before the nearby Long Biên Bridge, and it is still Hà Nội's largest covered market. After a fire gutted it in 1994, it was partly rebuilt in its original style.

challenge.title: Market challenge
challenge.text: At a market stall, start with "Chị ơi!" (to a woman seller) and ask "Bao nhiêu tiền?". Catch the number. If it sounds high, smile and say "Đắt quá!", then try "Rẻ hơn được không?" or "Bớt được không?" (can you knock a bit off?). Notice whether the seller drops the nghìn.
